claim_boundary: Eight assignments are analyst-reviewed from captured official PDFs and structured notes; claims are not independent reproductions.

rows.title: Extended High-frequency Cues to Phoneme Recognition: Insights from ASR
rows.semantic_reasoning: Extended high-frequency cues are tested as an acoustic factor in phoneme recognition under masking.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Problem: Speech in noise may depend on acoustic information above the frequency range normally used by speech systems. Mechanism: A neural network decodes phonemes from cochleagrams of broadband, 8-kHz-low-pass, and 6-kHz-low-pass speech under quiet and masked conditions. Result: Broadband speech improves phoneme accuracy in masked conditions, especially at lower TMR, while adding no quiet-condition benefit; removing extended high frequencies increases consonant omissions. Boundary: VCTK speech, selected maskers, cochleagram assumptions, and a model-based probe bound the conclusion; audiological benefit and general ASR deployment are not established.
rows.claim_boundary: Captured official PDF supports the structured note; results remain author-reported and were not independently reproduced.

rows.title: Room Impulse Response as a Prompt for Acoustic Echo Cancellation
rows.semantic_reasoning: Room impulse response prompts condition echo cancellation on the physical echo path to improve mismatch generalization.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Problem: Echo cancellation must work when the room's echo path differs from anything seen during training. Mechanism: ICCRN receives several RIR-prompt fusion variants; tests cover matched and mismatched synthetic RIRs plus recorded real RIRs in double-talk and far-end single-talk conditions. Result: Fusion method (d) is strongest on mismatched and real-RIR ICCRN tests; the reported real-RIR double-talk values are PESQ 2.19 and ERLE 4.79. Boundary: The selected model, fusion choices, RIRs, and author-reported tables bound the claim; independent reproduction and broad room coverage remain absent.
rows.claim_boundary: Captured official PDF supports the structured note; results remain author-reported and were not independently reproduced.

rows.title: Towards Multi-Level Transcript Segmentation: LoRA Fine-Tuning for Table-of-Contents Generation
rows.semantic_reasoning: Hierarchical transcript segmentation treats topic boundaries as nested sequence structure rather than flat cuts.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Problem: Long transcripts are easier to use when topics are organized into nested sections rather than one flat stream. Mechanism: TOC-NEMO uses LoRA fine-tuning and optional pause cues on AMI, VideoAula, and LectureDE; zero-shot prompting and supervised baselines provide comparisons. Result: Fine-tuned TOC-NEMO plus pause cues reports the strongest linear scores, including AMI F1 30.34/B 24.81 and VideoAula F1 67.34/B 55.18. Boundary: Datasets, prompts, annotations, and metric behavior constrain the result; transcript segmentation is not proof of human topic understanding.
rows.claim_boundary: Captured official PDF supports the structured note; results remain author-reported and were not independently reproduced.

rows.title: Efficient Streaming TTS Acoustic Model with Depthwise RVQ Decoding Strategies in a Mamba Framework
rows.semantic_reasoning: Depthwise codec decoding trades cross-level synthesis quality against streaming latency and model size.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Problem: A useful device speech generator must be intelligible, natural, fast enough for streaming, and usable across speakers. Mechanism: SMAM is tested with MLM, INR, and no-MLM decoding in a zero-shot speaker-conditioned setup; CER, similarity, quality, real-time factor, latency, and listening scores separate tradeoffs. Result: The proposed models are smaller and faster than listed non-streaming baselines while remaining competitive; removing MLM degrades quality measures. Boundary: Codec, datasets, hardware, and zero-shot speaker conditions bound the conclusion; other languages and devices are not established.
rows.claim_boundary: Captured official PDF supports the structured note; results remain author-reported and were not independently reproduced.

rows.title: Can ASR generate valid measures of child reading fluency?
rows.semantic_reasoning: ASR-derived child reading measures are checked against human-transcript measures to test whether automation preserves the educational construct.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Problem: Reading fluency assessment should capture accuracy, smoothness, phrasing, and pacing without manually scoring every child. Mechanism: The study evaluates 244 recordings from 131 Dutch children aged 6–13, compares four ASR systems, and correlates automatic and human-derived fluency measures. Result: The best reported system has WER 12.3% and timing F1 0.82; twelve measures meet r ≥ 0.7. Boundary: Dutch child reading, fixed texts, age distribution, ASR choice, and transcript comparison limit generalization; intervention or diagnosis validity is not established.
rows.claim_boundary: Captured official PDF supports the structured note; results remain author-reported and were not independently reproduced.

rows.title: PruneSLU: Efficient On-device Spoken Language Understanding through Vocabulary and Structural Pruning
rows.semantic_reasoning: Vocabulary-first and structural pruning preserve spoken-language-understanding task structure under device resource limits.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Problem: Spoken-language understanding must fit on a device with limited memory and power without losing needed intent and slot decisions. Mechanism: PruneSLU starts from Whisper-tiny, selects a base vocabulary, chooses layers by loss, and trains with language-model, distillation, and contrastive components on STOP and SLURP. Result: The 15M model retains 98% of original STOP performance, reaches STOP EM 72.31 and SLURP slot F1 71.42, and improves on listed compression baselines. Boundary: STOP/SLURP domains, Whisper initialization, five seeds, and author-reported comparisons bound the result; energy and open-world commands are not tested.
rows.claim_boundary: Captured official PDF supports the structured note; results remain author-reported and were not independently reproduced.

rows.title: AttentiveMOS: A Lightweight Attention-Only Model forSpeech Quality Prediction
rows.semantic_reasoning: A small attention model predicts listener quality while exposing how MOS prediction fails under domain shift.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Problem: A quality predictor should approximate what listeners hear without requiring a listening test for every utterance. Mechanism: AttentiveMOS uses Swin and transformer attention with 86K parameters and is evaluated across in-domain, out-of-domain, and cross-domain MOS datasets. Result: It beats listed lightweight baselines in the reported SOMOS-clean comparison, but PCC falls to 0.359 on out-of-domain LIVETALK. Boundary: MOS labels, listener composition, dataset domains, and the sharp shift drop limit claims of general quality assessment.
rows.claim_boundary: Captured official PDF supports the structured note; results remain author-reported and were not independently reproduced.

rows.title: Benchmarking Neural Speech Codec Intelligibility with SITool
rows.semantic_reasoning: Subjective intelligibility testing separates whether a codec preserves identifiable speech from whether it merely scores well on quality or WER.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Problem: A codec can sound pleasant yet make words harder to understand, so intelligibility needs its own evaluation target. Mechanism: SITool runs Diagnostic and Modified Rhyme Tests in laboratory or crowdsourcing settings; thirteen codecs are evaluated with phoneme, gender, and wordlist analyses. Result: Some neural codecs outperform traditional codecs in subjective intelligibility, but objective agreement varies and scores show gender- and wordlist-specific differences. Boundary: The codec set, English tests, listener screening, and objective metrics bound the conclusion; the toolkit does not remove human evaluation.
